Almost every Ukrainian oblast is named for its capital city, so the hook
is usually the city's own name - and those are mostly rivers, founders or
Cossack history. Two words open a lot of them:
The map has both Kyiv the city and Kyiv Oblast around it, with separate
ids, so each gets its own entry. Crimea and Sevastopol are on the map
because Natural Earth files them under Ukraine; DECISIONS.md records that
Ids drop the diacritics and apostrophes, e.g. Khmelnytskyi is
chernihiv: Probably from chornyi, "black" — the dark soil or the dark woods around it.
One of the oldest cities in the country, and its Saviour Cathedral was begun before 1036, older than anything standing in Kyiv.
sumy: From sumka, a bag or pouch: legend says three hunting bags were found at the founding, and the city's arms show three of them.
Founded in 1655 by Cossacks moving east away from Polish rule.
volyn: Named for a vanished town, Volyn, and the Volhynians who lived around it — a name recorded in the eleventh century.
Lutsk's castle here has stood since the 1340s, and is on the 200-hryvnia note.
rivne: From rivnyi, "flat" or "even" — the ground around the town.
It was Polish between the wars and had one of the largest Jewish communities in Volhynia before 1941.
zhytomyr: Most likely from a founder's name, Zhytomyr — zhyto also means rye, so the folk reading is "rye and peace".
Korolev, who built the rockets that launched Sputnik and Gagarin, was born here.
kyiv: Named for Kyi, the eldest of three brothers who legend says founded the city with their sister Lybid.
The Kyivan Rus state here was the origin of both Ukraine and Russia, which is why the name carries the weight it does.
kyiv-oblast: The region around the capital, named for it — the city itself is administered separately and appears on this map on its own.
Chornobyl is in this oblast, and the exclusion zone around it has become, unintentionally, one of Europe's largest wildlife refuges.
lviv: "Lev's city" — King Danylo of Galicia founded it around 1250 and named it for his son Lev.
Austrian until 1918 and Polish until 1939, it is the most central-European city in Ukraine, down to the coffee houses.
poltava: From the river Ltava, with the prefix po-, "along" — the settlement by the Ltava.
Peter the Great beat the Swedes here in 1709, ending Sweden's time as a great power.
khmelnytskyi: Renamed in 1954 for Bohdan Khmelnytskyi, the Cossack hetman; before that it was Proskuriv.
His 1648 uprising against Poland created a Cossack state and is the founding story of modern Ukraine.
kharkiv: Named for the river Kharkiv, which may itself come from a semi-legendary Cossack founder called Kharko.
It was the capital of Soviet Ukraine until 1934, which is why it has the constructivist Derzhprom, one of the first skyscrapers in Europe.
ternopil: Ternovyi pil, "thorn field" — the blackthorn scrub the town was built on.
Its lake is artificial and four centuries old, dug as part of the town's defences.
cherkasy: From the Cherkasy, an old name for the Cossacks — possibly linked to the Circassians of the Caucasus.
The Dnipro widens into the Kremenchuk Reservoir here, 250 km long and the largest body of water in the country.
vinnytsya: Probably from vino, an old Slavic word for a dowry or tribute paid in land.
Hitler's Werwolf headquarters was built in the forest outside the city, and he spent months of 1942 and 1943 there.
luhansk: From the river Luhan, itself from luh, a water meadow.
Founded in 1795 around a British-built cannon foundry, to arm the Black Sea fleet.
ivano-frankivsk: Renamed in 1962 for the poet Ivan Franko; for three centuries before that it was Stanislaviv, after the founder's son.
The gateway to the Carpathians and the Hutsul highlands, whose music and woodwork are unlike anything else in the country.
kirovohrad: The map's name is the Soviet one, for Sergei Kirov; since 2016 it has been Kropyvnytskyi, after a playwright.
It was founded as Fort St Elizabeth in 1754, and has been renamed five times.
zakarpattia: "Beyond the Carpathians" — za is beyond, and it is the only Ukrainian region on the far side of the mountains.
Hungarian for a thousand years, then Czechoslovak, then Soviet; it still has Hungarian, Romanian and Rusyn villages.
dnipropetrovsk: The Dnipro plus Grigory Petrovsky, a Soviet official; the city dropped the second half in 2016 and is now simply Dnipro.
It was Katerynoslav first, "Catherine's glory", founded by Potemkin for Catherine the Great.
chernivtsi: From chornyi, "black", and a fortress of black wood or black earth on the Prut.
Austrian until 1918, and so mixed that its university was German, its theatre Romanian and its poets — Paul Celan among them — wrote in German.
donetsk: From the Siverskyi Donets river; donets is a little Don.
Founded in 1869 by a Welsh ironmaster, John Hughes, and called Yuzivka — a Russian rendering of his name — for fifty years.
mykolayiv: For St Nicholas, patron of sailors: the shipyard was founded on his feast day in 1789.
Most of the Soviet Union's aircraft carriers were built here, on a river 100 km from the sea.
zaporizhzhya: Za porohamy, "beyond the rapids" — the Dnipro cataracts that the Cossack Sich sat below.
The rapids themselves are gone, drowned by the 1932 dam that made the reservoir.
odesa: Named in 1795 after Odessos, a Greek colony thought to have stood nearby — it did not, but the name stayed.
A free port for its first sixty years, which is why it filled with Greeks, Italians, Jews and Frenchmen and sounds unlike anywhere else in Ukraine.
kherson: For Chersonesos, the Greek city in Crimea — Catherine the Great liked classical names and used them across the south.
The first Black Sea shipyard was here, before Mykolayiv and before Sevastopol.
crimea: From Qirim, the Crimean Tatar name of the old capital; the Greeks had called the peninsula Tauris.
Greeks, Scythians, Goths, Genoese, Tatars, Ottomans and Russians have all held it, and the Tatars were deported wholesale in 1944.
sevastopol: Greek again, coined in 1783: sebastos, "venerable", plus polis — one of Catherine's classical inventions.
Besieged for eleven months in the Crimean War and eight in the Second World War.
